source_refs.note: Exercise 14.4 Q6 (a)(i)-(iv), (b), book p.290 (PDF 295). Answer key PDF 312: (a) 4, 3, 1, 0, correct (sympy); (b) proof, no key. Solution book PDF 1276-1278 agrees.

blocks.explanation:
A value of a scalar triple product of unit vectors.
We must find one number.
Plan: the cross is done first, then the dot; pull the numbers 2 and 2 outside.
steps:
Given: \(2\underline{i} \times 2\underline{j} \cdot \underline{k}\).
To find: its value.
Method: it means \((2\underline{i} \times 2\underline{j}) \cdot \underline{k}\); scalars can be taken out of cross and dot products.

Work it out
\[(2\underline{i} \times 2\underline{j}) \cdot \underline{k} = 4(\underline{i} \times \underline{j}) \cdot \underline{k}\]
\[= 4\,\underline{k} \cdot \underline{k} = 4(1) = 4\]
Why: \(\underline{i}, \underline{j}, \underline{k}\) follow the cycle \(\underline{i} \to \underline{j} \to \underline{k} \to \underline{i}\): \(\underline{i} \times \underline{j} = \underline{k}\), \(\underline{j} \times \underline{k} = \underline{i}\), \(\underline{k} \times \underline{i} = \underline{j}\); and \(\underline{i} \cdot \underline{i} = \underline{j} \cdot \underline{j} = \underline{k} \cdot \underline{k} = 1\).

Check
\[[\underline{i}\ \underline{j}\ \underline{k}] = 1 \Rightarrow 4[\underline{i}\ \underline{j}\ \underline{k}] = 4 \;\checkmark\]
Why: \((\underline{i} \times \underline{j}) \cdot \underline{k}\) is \([\underline{i}\ \underline{j}\ \underline{k}]\), the volume of the unit cube.

blocks.explanation:
Again a triple product of unit vectors.
We must find one number.
Plan: cross first: \(\underline{k} \times \underline{i}\), then dot with \(3\underline{j}\).
steps:
Given: \(3\underline{j} \cdot \underline{k} \times \underline{i}\).
To find: its value.
Method: it means \(3\underline{j} \cdot (\underline{k} \times \underline{i})\).

Work it out
\[\underline{k} \times \underline{i} = \underline{j}\]
\[3\underline{j} \cdot \underline{j} = 3(1) = 3\]
Why: \(\underline{i}, \underline{j}, \underline{k}\) follow the cycle \(\underline{i} \to \underline{j} \to \underline{k} \to \underline{i}\): \(\underline{i} \times \underline{j} = \underline{k}\), \(\underline{j} \times \underline{k} = \underline{i}\), \(\underline{k} \times \underline{i} = \underline{j}\); and \(\underline{i} \cdot \underline{i} = \underline{j} \cdot \underline{j} = \underline{k} \cdot \underline{k} = 1\).

Check
\[3[\underline{j}\ \underline{k}\ \underline{i}] = 3[\underline{i}\ \underline{j}\ \underline{k}] = 3 \;\checkmark\]
Why: \(\underline{j}, \underline{k}, \underline{i}\) is a cyclic shift of \(\underline{i}, \underline{j}, \underline{k}\), which does not change the triple product.

blocks.explanation:
The bracket \([\underline{a}\ \underline{b}\ \underline{c}]\) means \(\underline{a} \cdot (\underline{b} \times \underline{c})\).
We must find one number.
Plan: write it as \(\underline{k} \cdot (\underline{i} \times \underline{j})\).
steps:
Given: \([\underline{k}\ \underline{i}\ \underline{j}]\).
To find: its value.
Method: \([\underline{k}\ \underline{i}\ \underline{j}] = \underline{k} \cdot (\underline{i} \times \underline{j})\).

Work it out
\[\underline{i} \times \underline{j} = \underline{k}\]
\[\underline{k} \cdot \underline{k} = 1\]
Why: \(\underline{i}, \underline{j}, \underline{k}\) follow the cycle \(\underline{i} \to \underline{j} \to \underline{k} \to \underline{i}\): \(\underline{i} \times \underline{j} = \underline{k}\), \(\underline{j} \times \underline{k} = \underline{i}\), \(\underline{k} \times \underline{i} = \underline{j}\); and \(\underline{i} \cdot \underline{i} = \underline{j} \cdot \underline{j} = \underline{k} \cdot \underline{k} = 1\).

Check
\[\begin{vmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{vmatrix} = 1(1 - 0) = 1 \;\checkmark\]
Why: The components of \(\underline{k}, \underline{i}, \underline{j}\) as rows; only the corner entry 1 gives a non-zero term.

blocks.explanation:
A triple product in which one vector is repeated.
We must find one number.
Plan: \(\underline{i} \cdot (\underline{i} \times \underline{k})\); \(\underline{i} \times \underline{k}\) is perpendicular to \(\underline{i}\).
steps:
Given: \([\underline{i}\ \underline{i}\ \underline{k}]\).
To find: its value.
Method: \([\underline{i}\ \underline{i}\ \underline{k}] = \underline{i} \cdot (\underline{i} \times \underline{k})\).

Work it out
\[\underline{i} \times \underline{k} = -\underline{j}\]
\[\underline{i} \cdot (-\underline{j}) = 0\]
Why: \(\underline{k} \times \underline{i} = \underline{j}\), so \(\underline{i} \times \underline{k} = -\underline{j}\) (reversing the order changes the sign). \(\underline{i}\) and \(\underline{j}\) are perpendicular, so their dot product is 0.

Check
\[\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 0 \;\checkmark\]
Why: A determinant with two equal rows is 0. In general, a triple product with a repeated vector is always 0 (the three vectors are coplanar).

blocks.explanation:
A proof using the cyclic property of the scalar triple product.
We must show the left side equals \(3\underline{u} \cdot (\underline{v} \times \underline{w})\).
Plan: rewrite the second and third terms as \([\underline{u}\ \underline{v}\ \underline{w}]\) by cyclic shifts, then add.
steps:
Given: any three vectors \(\underline{u}, \underline{v}, \underline{w}\).
To prove: L.H.S. \(= 3\underline{u} \cdot (\underline{v} \times \underline{w})\).
Method: cyclic property: \([\underline{u}\ \underline{v}\ \underline{w}] = [\underline{v}\ \underline{w}\ \underline{u}] = [\underline{w}\ \underline{u}\ \underline{v}]\).

Write each term as a bracket
\[\underline{v} \cdot (\underline{w} \times \underline{u}) = [\underline{v}\ \underline{w}\ \underline{u}]\]
\[\underline{w} \cdot (\underline{u} \times \underline{v}) = [\underline{w}\ \underline{u}\ \underline{v}]\]
Why: \(\underline{a} \cdot (\underline{b} \times \underline{c}) = [\underline{a}\ \underline{b}\ \underline{c}]\) by definition.

Use the cyclic property
\[[\underline{v}\ \underline{w}\ \underline{u}] = [\underline{u}\ \underline{v}\ \underline{w}]\]
\[[\underline{w}\ \underline{u}\ \underline{v}] = [\underline{u}\ \underline{v}\ \underline{w}]\]
Why: Moving the vectors round the cycle \(\underline{u} \to \underline{v} \to \underline{w} \to \underline{u}\) does not change the value (it is the same determinant with its rows shifted twice, and each shift by two row swaps keeps the sign).

Add the three terms
\[\text{L.H.S.} = [\underline{u}\ \underline{v}\ \underline{w}] + [\underline{u}\ \underline{v}\ \underline{w}] + [\underline{u}\ \underline{v}\ \underline{w}]\]
\[= 3[\underline{u}\ \underline{v}\ \underline{w}]\]
\[= 3\underline{u} \cdot (\underline{v} \times \underline{w}) = \text{R.H.S.}\]
Why: Three equal numbers add to three times one of them.
